# Volume 3 — Chapter XXXI Nell to Cressida

!!! note "Source text"
    Passages cited on the wiki pages link into this page. Only volumes at or before
    this page's cutoff are present.

“Nell Harcourt sends greetings to Cressida Lindsay.
{: #nw-v03-c31-p0000 }

“Dearest, I really ought to have written to you before now. In this place, I have settled in again to the life of a rural ‘schoolma’am’ located at Coombe Road, taking up lodging at ‘Wayside,’ which belongs to Miss Thora Sweet. Thora is an affectionate person who possesses very attractive looks; her height is tall, though not excessively so; she is somewhat plump, but retains a particular control of silhouette that implies a frugal spirit who will not be overly generous even regarding body weight. A bun of soft, wavy, brown hair containing a strand of grey adorns her head, above a cheerful face boasting pink cheeks, along with large, gentle eyes that match the blueness of forget-me-nots. Furthermore, she belongs to that charming, traditional class of cooks who are completely unconcerned about ruining your stomach provided that they can supply you with luxurious banquets.
{: #nw-v03-c31-p0001 }

“She is to my liking; and I am to hers—mainly, it appears, for the reason that a sister of hers called Nell passed away at an early age.
{: #nw-v03-c31-p0002 }

“‘It makes me truly happy to meet you,’ she remarked with energy upon my arrival in her yard. ‘Goodness, my expectations of your appearance were completely off. I felt certain your hair would be dark—darkness was a trait of my sister Nell. Yet red is the color of yours!’
{: #nw-v03-c31-p0003 }

“At first, I believed my initial expectation of Thora might not hold, and that I would dislike her for a brief time. Shortly after, I told myself I ought to act more reasonably instead of holding a grudge against a person merely for labeling my hair red. It was likely that Thora did not even have the word ‘auburn’ in her vocabulary.
{: #nw-v03-c31-p0004 }

“‘Wayside’ is a charming kind of small place. Set down in a lovely little depression that slopes down from the road, the home is white and small. An orchard and flower-garden, completely blended together, lie between the house and the road. Quahog clam-shells—which Thora refers to as ‘cow-hawks’—border the walk to the front door; Virginia Creeper grows over the porch, and moss covers the roof. Located ‘off the parlor,’ my room is a tidy little space—containing just enough room for me and the bed. A picture hangs over the head of my bed showing Robby Burns as he stands at Highland Mary’s grave, shaded by a huge weeping willow tree. Because Robby’s face looks so mournful, it is not surprising that I experience nightmares. Indeed, during my initial night in this place, I had a dream where laughing was impossible for me.
{: #nw-v03-c31-p0005 }

“The parlor is small and tidy. A massive willow heavily shades its single window, giving the room a cave-like appearance of green darkness. Fantastic tidies rest on the chairs, colorful mats lie on the floor, books and cards are neatly set out on a circular table, and containers of dried grass sit on the mantel-piece. Positioned between the containers is a bright ornament made of saved coffin plates—a total of five, belonging individually to the father of Thora, her mother, a brother, her sister Nell, and a farmhand who once passed away in this place! Should I unexpectedly lose my mind one of these days ‘know all men by these presents’ that my madness was brought on by those coffin-plates.
{: #nw-v03-c31-p0006 }

“However, every bit of it is wonderful, and I expressed that very thought. Thora adored me on account of it, in the exact manner that she loathed unfortunate Esther for having remarked that an excessive amount of shade was unsanitary and for refusing to rest upon a feather bed. As for me, I delight in feather-beds, and my delight increases the more unsanitary and filled with feathers they become. Thora mentions that observing me dine brings her great solace; she was terribly worried that I might resemble Miss Haythorne, who refused every food except fruit and warm water when eating breakfast and attempted to persuade Thora to abandon frying food. In truth, Esther is a sweet young woman, yet she possesses a habit of following whims. Her difficulty stems from a lack of creativity combined with an inclination toward indigestion.
{: #nw-v03-c31-p0007 }

“I was informed by Thora that the parlor was available to me whenever any young men visited! However, I doubt there are numerous ones to visit. No young man has been seen by me in Coombe Road so far, with the exception of the hired boy next door—Sam Toliver, a youth who is very tall, lank, and tow-haired. A short time ago, he came over one evening to sit for an hour on the garden fence, close to the front porch where fancy-work was being done by Thora and me. During that entire duration, the sole comments offered by him were, ‘Hev a peppermint, miss! Dew now-fine thing for cararrh, peppermints,’ and, ‘Powerful lot o’ jump-grasses round here ternight. Yep.’
{: #nw-v03-c31-p0008 }

“Yet a romantic involvement is taking place right here. Appearing to be involved, to a greater or lesser degree, in late-life romances seems to be my destiny. That their wedding was caused by me is something Mr. and Mrs. Stanhope constantly claim. Continuing to be exceedingly thankful to me for an idea that another person would likely have offered had I not done so is Mrs. Stephen Clark of Delford. Nevertheless, it is my genuine belief that, had I not assisted him and Theodora Dix, Ludovic Speed would have made no additional progress beyond serene courting.
{: #nw-v03-c31-p0009 }

“Regarding the current matter, my role is merely that of a passive observer. Having attempted to assist once before, I caused a dreadful disaster. Consequently, I will refrain from further interference. When we see each other, I will share the entire story with you.”
{: #nw-v03-c31-p0010 }
